issues.legal_issue: A criminal prosecution arising from a commercial contract may not be quashed solely because the dispute also has a civil remedy or is subject to arbitration when the allegations prima facie disclose criminal offences.
material_facts: The complaint, FIR and charge-sheet alleged that the seller obtained substantial payments under an agreement to sell, failed to complete required steps, withheld material information about the property's mortgage and its discharge, and later terminated the agreement.
The charge-sheet also referred to alleged conduct concerning the property's subdivision and an earlier transaction involving the same property.
The High Court quashed the proceedings on the grounds that the dispute arose from a terminated contract and arbitration was pending.
The Supreme Court found that the allegations could disclose the ingredients of cheating and criminal breach of trust, while leaving their truth to be determined at trial.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in quashing the criminal proceedings merely because the transaction was commercial, the agreement had been terminated, or arbitration was pending; the appeal was allowed and the proceedings restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 CrPC, inherent powers are extraordinary and must be used with care, consistently with the illustrative categories in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal. A commercial transaction may also involve an offence, and arbitration does not substitute for criminal prosecution of an alleged offence: Trisuns Chemical Industry v. Rajesh Agarwal. Whether allegations are true is ordinarily for trial, not a reason to quash where the complaint discloses an offence: Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. P. Radhakrishna. The Court also referred to the illustrations of cheating in Sections 415, 418 and 420 IPC and considered the alleged offences under Sections 406, 420 and 34 IPC.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_appeal and allegations_prima_facie_disclose_offence and (commercial_transaction or civil_remedy_available or arbitration_pending)

predicates.criminal_quashing_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order that quashed criminal proceedings.
predicates.allegations_prima_facie_disclose_offence: The complaint, FIR or charge-sheet alleges facts that, taken at face value, may satisfy the elements of a criminal offence.
predicates.commercial_transaction: The alleged conduct arose in the course of a commercial transaction.
predicates.civil_remedy_available: The parties have a civil remedy concerning the same dispute.
predicates.arbitration_pending: Arbitral proceedings concerning the dispute have been initiated or are pending.
predicates.criminal_proceedings_must_not_be_quashed: The criminal proceedings are not to be quashed solely because the dispute is commercial, a civil remedy exists, or arbitration is pending.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges quashing and the allegations may disclose an offence, the commercial or civil character of the dispute, or pending arbitration, does not by itself justify quashing the criminal proceedings.

issues.legal_issue: At the quashing stage, the court must assess the complaint, FIR, charge-sheet and supporting material on their face without deciding the truth of the allegations or accepting disputed defence material as conclusive.
material_facts: A charge-sheet had been filed and placed before the High Court, but the High Court's decision did not examine it and focused on the agreement, its termination and the pending arbitration.
The complaint, FIR and charge-sheet contained allegations which the Supreme Court considered capable of disclosing offences.

The respondent relied on documentary material and argued that the agreement had been terminated because of the complainant's breach; the Supreme Court held that this defence was not for the High Court to decide when considering quashing.
The Supreme Court held that the truth or falsity of the allegations was to be determined on evidence at trial.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not quash the proceedings by overlooking the charge-sheet or resolving disputed factual matters; the allegations and materials had to be considered on their face, with their truth left to trial.
issues.legal_principle: The inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC requires examination of the complaint, FIR, charge-sheet and relevant material as presented, without a critical determination of their truth. The categories in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal guide, but do not exhaust, the circumstances for quashing. Arnab Manoranjan Goswami v. State of Maharashtra was cited on the contours of the jurisdiction, and Nagpur Steel & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. P. Radhakrishna supports leaving the truth of allegations to trial where an offence is disclosed.

predicates.criminal_quashing_proceeding: The court is considering whether to quash a criminal complaint, FIR or prosecution.
predicates.face_value_material_discloses_offence: The allegations and accompanying material, taken at face value, disclose a possible criminal offence.
predicates.disputed_truth_or_defence_requires_evide: The accused disputes the allegations or relies on a defence whose correctness depends on resolving facts or evidence.
predicates.court_must_leave_disputed_truth_for_tria: The court must not determine the disputed truth or defence at the quashing stage and must leave it for trial.

issues.definition: If face-value material in a quashing proceeding discloses an offence and resolving the defence requires evidence, the court leaves that dispute for trial.

issues.legal_issue: A matter need not be remitted for reconsideration of a quashing order when the parties have fully argued the case and the appellate record contains sufficient material to decide it, particularly when remand would delay the trial.
material_facts: The respondent argued that the matter should be remitted because the High Court had not considered the charge-sheet and other material.
The parties had argued the matter fully before the Supreme Court and taken the Court through the criminal record.
The Supreme Court found sufficient material in that record to connect the respondent with the alleged crime and considered remand futile and likely to delay the trial.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to remit the matter to the High Court and decided the appeal on the record before it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its appellate discretion to avoid a futile remand where the matter had been fully argued and the record was sufficient to decide the challenge, taking account of the need not to delay the criminal trial. No earlier case was relied on for this specific remand decision.

rule.if: appeal_from_quashing_order and parties_fully_argued and appellate_record_sufficient and remand_would_delay_trial

predicates.appeal_from_quashing_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order quashing a criminal prosecution.
predicates.parties_fully_argued: The parties have fully presented their arguments to the appellate court.
predicates.appellate_record_sufficient: The record before the appellate court contains sufficient material to decide the challenge.
predicates.remand_would_delay_trial: Sending the matter back would cause avoidable delay to the criminal trial.
predicates.court_may_decide_without_remand: The appellate court may decide the challenge without remitting the matter for reconsideration.

issues.definition: When a quashing appeal has been fully argued, the record is sufficient, and remand would delay trial, the appellate court may decide the matter without remitting it.

issues.legal_issue: An application seeking proceedings for alleged false statements or concealment may be dismissed when the court finds that it was made for ulterior reasons.
material_facts: At the conclusion of the appeal, the respondent filed an application under Sections 340 and 195 CrPC alleging that the appellants had concealed documents and made false statements.
The Supreme Court found that such applications were being filed for ulterior reasons and dismissed the application.
issues.conclusion: The application was dismissed, and the Court deprecated the filing of such applications for ulterior reasons.
issues.legal_principle: The application invoked Sections 340 and 195 CrPC. The Court dismissed it on its finding that it had been filed for ulterior reasons; it did not set out a broader test for applications under those provisions.

predicates.criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal.
predicates.application_seeks_false_statement_procee: A party applies for proceedings based on alleged false statements or concealment in court proceedings.
predicates.court_finds_ulterior_purpose: The court finds that the application was made for an ulterior purpose.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal, when an application seeking proceedings over alleged false statements or concealment is found to have an ulterior purpose, it is dismissed.
